title: Saudi capital’s airport to remain shut this week as airlines cancel services
summary: Lufthansa Group canceled all flights to Riyadh until October 16, while Air France-KLM has extended a suspension to and from Riyadh until the end of October

items: Riyadh's international airport closure has been extended until October 17 due to ongoing attacks by Yemen's Houthis, leading to widespread flight cancellations.
The attacks, including a ballistic missile strike on the airport, have resulted in significant casualties and raised concerns about the safety of civil aviation in the region.
Airlines globally are suspending services to Saudi Arabia, with the disruptions impacting the country's economy and scheduled events, including major conferences.

Authorities have extended the closure of Riyadh’s international airport until Saturday, October 17, and airlines scrapped flights after continuing attacks by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis emptied the skies over Saudi Arabia’s capital.

Operations at King Khalid International Airport, Saudi Arabia’s second-busiest airport after Jeddah, were suspended to “allow for the completion of procedures to ensure the safety and operational readiness of the airport’s facilities,” the Saudi civil aviation authority said in a statement.

Late on Monday, the Houthis said they had attacked the airport with a ballistic missile, shortly after Saudi Arabia said it had intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile fired by the group towards Riyadh.
The Houthis also said in a statement that they targeted an airbase in Khamis Mushait in the kingdom’s southwest with a drone. There was no immediate Saudi confirmation.
A Notice to Airmen issued on Monday showed King Khalid International Airport will stay closed until 2100 GMT on October 17.

The airport has been shut since an attack on Saturday that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300, the deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade. On Sunday, another attack killed one person and injured nearly a dozen others.

The attacks marked one of the most significant disruptions to Saudi aviation in years, adding to pressures on an industry already grappling with conflict across the Middle East and with higher jet fuel prices that are eating into profits.
They have also raised worries over civil aviation becoming a target in armed conflict.
“This level of sustained intense attack on civil aviation is unprecedented,” said Mark Zee, founder of OPSGROUP, a membership-based organization that provides aviation safety advice.
“I think this requires us to rethink how we view the current risk picture, and tread very carefully,” he said.
Air traffic tracker Flightradar24 showed planes avoiding the city on Monday, though jets were crossing Saudi airspace and landing at top hub Jeddah on the country’s west coast.
Cancellations across all Saudi airports reached 46.4%, aviation analytics firm Cirium said.

The disruption has forced airlines across Europe and Asia to suspend services, while the Federal Aviation Administration advised US carriers on Sunday to exercise caution when flying to or over Saudi Arabia. EU aviation body EASA widened a Saudi airspace warning on Friday, citing missile and drone attacks.
“The impact goes beyond Saudi Arabia to the wider region and to its global connections,” said aviation analyst John Strickland.
OPSGROUP advised airlines to avoid the southern aviation corridor over the Middle East altogether, and take a route from Europe to Asia over central Asia.
That adds “extensive distance” for some routes and “closes off options for getting into Dubai, Abu Dhabi for most western carriers,” Zee said.
Lufthansa Group canceled all flights to Riyadh until October 16, while Air France-KLM has extended a suspension to and from Riyadh until the end of the month.

Etihad Airways said it had canceled flights between Abu Dhabi and Riyadh, Jeddah and Dammam due to “regional disruption,” adding that all flights between Abu Dhabi and Riyadh would be canceled until October 19.
Qatar Airways said on Monday it had temporarily suspended flights to and from Riyadh and Dammam due to the “current situation.”
Delta Air Lines said it was delaying planned services from Atlanta to Riyadh, initially due to start on October 23, until March 2027.

The escalation with the Houthis has raised concerns over the broader economic impact. Saudi Arabia’s real GDP is projected to contract by 3.6% this year, reflecting a combination of factors including lower oil activity.

The attacks have put events scheduled in Riyadh this month under pressure, including the kingdom’s flagship investment conference and the WPC Energy Congress, where several top oil executives were dropped from the program. – Rappler.com
